name: Yara Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a roof-bolting crew underground at a large nickel mine and operate the bolter when the roof is uneven. The machine drills a hole and sets a steel bolt so rock stays above us; I check the pattern against the face before anyone moves forward. A two-year technical diploma taught me the measurements, and long experience taught me which crack matters. My partner Nabil repairs bicycles, our children are grown, and our house is paid for. We have about sixteen months of expenses saved and hope I can retire at 67. I use AI every day to compare bolt tension notes, then inspect the roof myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker bolt log helps if it leaves more time to look up at the roof. A loose rock is still above the roof-bolting crew when a computer finishes sorting numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead wage will keep coming and Nabil's bicycle work will add something, though repair orders vary. Our paid house and sixteen months saved make the mild picture manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking the first bolt pattern by eye and use my AI tool to sort tension readings after each shift. In the first year I'll show apprentices how I compare a software warning with the torque gauge before signing the log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our wages. I like a small tool that keeps a safety record clear without taking the drill from my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a software warning mislead you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software once marked a bolt low because a gauge reading was entered twice. I checked the gauge and the rock before sending the crew back to tighten it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would household saving change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nabil we can keep the retirement transfer and the trip to see our grown children. I wouldn't spend the reserve just because the log is quicker.

say: I would welcome a **quicker bolt log** while keeping eyes on the roof.
I would tell apprentices to **check the torque gauge** before signing a software warning.
think: I expect my **lead wage** and Nabil’s bicycle repairs to continue.
I think our **paid house** and sixteen months saved make this change manageable.
do: **Keep checking** the first bolt pattern by eye before the crew advances.
**Teach apprentices** to compare AI tension warnings with the torque gauge.
feel: **Calm** about wages and pleased by clearer safety records.
S0.quote: A loose rock is still above the roof-bolting crew when a computer finishes sorting numbers.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** remains tied to a torque gauge and an actual roof check.
A **sixteen-month cushion** and paid home protect the household in the modest-change picture.

steps.text: Keep inspecting the first roof-bolt pattern before the crew advances

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and supply orders will move to software before a robot can read a roof and set bolts. Let the bolting crew compare any new pattern with the cracks they can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the planning desk may get smaller, and managers could expect more metres bolted each hour. My lead wage should hold, but a rushed pattern can leave the next crew under a weak patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll test the pattern tool against three old roof maps this month and mark any bolt line that crosses a known fracture. In the first year I'll take those marks to the supervisor and ask for a crew check before the plan reaches the bolter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious and uneasy. I can afford to stop a shift, but an apprentice may feel pressured to keep the machine moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bolt pattern would you reject?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the new plan leaves too much space between bolts under a fractured roof, I will stop the bolter. A faster roof-bolt pattern does not make broken mine rock whole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How should a new operator challenge your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the youngest operator to bring me a wrong bolt line even if I approved the draft. Being experienced means listening when somebody else sees a crack.

say: I would expect **planning and supplies** to change before robots set roof bolts.
I would give the **bolting crew** a check on software patterns before drilling.
think: I expect my **lead pay** to hold while planning jobs change.
I worry **faster metre targets** could leave apprentices under weak rock.
do: **Test pattern software** against three previous roof maps this month.
**Bring fracture marks** to the supervisor and require a crew check before drilling.
feel: **Curious** about the tool and uneasy about pressure on apprentices.
S1.quote: A faster roof-bolt pattern does not make broken mine rock whole.
fieldNote: She tests **thinking tools** against known fractures, rather than treating software lines as instructions.
Her **own wage feels secure**; she worries about newer operators being pressed to advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could rewrite bolt plans, while capable bolting robots follow around 2031. We need paid practical training before anyone is told a robot makes their shift unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, four years before I hope to retire. Our sixteen months of savings cannot replace four years of roof-bolting wages and pension contributions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll register for the mine's existing remote-bolter course this winter if it includes live roof practice and the mine pays the fee. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll seek a posted remote-bolter job only if its wage stays near my lead pay and I can stop the machine from the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a four-year gap, though I can learn the new work. I would rather train on a real bolter than ask our grown children to fill our pension account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect the reserve during training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nabil we will keep the sixteen-month reserve untouched while I train, provided my mine wages continue. Bicycle repair orders can fall in a wet month, so I will not count them as a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a remote course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the instructor to show a real stop when a bolt starts to split the roof. If the course is only a video, I will keep my paid shifts and look for another practical course.

say: I would separate **2028 bolt planning** from capable bolting robots around 2031.
I would ask for **paid practical training** before robot systems remove shifts.
think: I think at **63**, I could lose four earning years before planned retirement at 67.
I think sixteen months saved cannot replace **pension contributions**.
do: **Take remote-bolter training** this winter only with mine-paid fees, live roof practice and maintained wages.
**Seek** a posted remote-bolter job after thinking AI arrives only with near-lead pay and stop authority.
feel: **Anxious** about a four-year income gap, while ready to learn practical controls.
S2.quote: Our sixteen months of savings cannot replace four years of roof-bolting wages and pension contributions.
fieldNote: Her **2031 age** is 63, four years ahead of hoped-for retirement at 67.
Training needs **mine-paid fees**, live practice and maintained wages; a job move needs a posting, near-lead pay and stop authority.

steps.text: Take remote-bolter training if mine pays fees, provides live roof practice and maintains wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes bolt plans first, while capable bolting robots arrive around 2034. A few years should let us test the equipment on a real roof before it becomes a shift rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots arrive, one year before I hope to retire. Our reserve could cover that year, but I would rather earn the last pension contribution if a real controls post exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll take supervised remote-bolter practice if the mine offers a paid place. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll apply for a posted controls role if it keeps near-lead pay and lets me stop a bolter when the roof shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert and a bit anxious about that last year of pay. The extra warning is useful only if the work and wage are stated plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the controls post does not exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no controls post exists, I would keep leading the roof crew while those shifts last and ask the retirement office for pension figures at 66 and 67. I will not spend our roof-bolting savings reserve before seeing what the mine pension pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell your children a date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children the retirement date when Nabil and I have the written figures. I don't want them planning around a course I may not get into.

say: I would use the **2034 robot date** to test remote bolting on a real roof.
I would require a **posted wage** and stop authority before changing roles.
think: I think at **66**, robots could cost my last planned year of work.
I think our **sixteen-month reserve** could bridge a year, but I prefer a real controls wage.
do: **Take supervised practice** this year only if the mine offers a paid place.
**Apply** for a posted controls role after thinking AI arrives only with near-lead pay and bolter stop authority.
feel: **Anxious** about one year of pay, with savings and time to test a role.
S3.quote: I will not spend our roof-bolting savings reserve before seeing what the mine pension pays.
fieldNote: Her **2034 age** is 66, one year before hoped-for retirement.
The **training place** must be paid, and the controls application needs a real posting, near-lead wage and stop authority.

steps.text: Take supervised remote-bolter practice if the mine offers a paid place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2036 changes plans, while capable bolting robots come around 2039. I hope to be retired by then, though new operators should still get proper supervised practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. Our paid house and sixteen months saved make retirement at 67 plausible if the written pension covers our ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading safe bolting shifts and paying into retirement while the roster lasts. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if retired as planned, I'll review the pension budget with Nabil and offer one supervised practice day at the mine training bay if they invite me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our own work and money in this picture. I would enjoy watching a new operator learn the first safe stop on a real machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if pension income is too low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension is lower than we expect, I would apply for a posted roof-bolting shift at a nearby mine before draining savings. I would need an actual offer with workable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new operator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentices to mark every unusual crack, even when a pattern screen shows nothing. A careful roof-bolter can stop a machine before a poor bolt reaches the next crew.

I would keep **supervised machine practice** in the mine’s apprentice training.
think: I think at **68 and 71**, I expect retirement if written pension income covers bills.
I think our **paid house and reserve** give room without replacing a pension.

feel: **Calm** about household income, with interest in teaching safe stops to apprentices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable bolting robots around 2031 could cost four years of pay before my planned retirement. A paid live-roof course and a posted remote-bolter role with real stop authority would let me keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who will stand beside a new roof-bolter for the first bad hole. A skilled operator must stand beside a new roof-bolter when the first bolt turns badly. A screen cannot reach up and feel the bolt turn.

headlineQuote: A skilled operator must stand beside a new roof-bolter when the first bolt turns badly.
portrait: **Yara Farah**, 58, leads roof bolting at a large nickel mine and holds a two-year technical diploma.
She uses **AI daily** for bolt tension notes, then checks the torque gauge and roof herself.
Her **higher wage**, paid home and sixteen months saved support retirement hopes alongside her partner’s variable bicycle repair income.
She hopes to **retire at 67**, so 2031 robots at 63 threaten four earning years and 2034 robots at 66 threaten one.
She seeks **paid live-roof training** and posted controls work only with near-lead pay and stop authority.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable bolting robots could arrive four years before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid practical course** and posted remote-bolter work with stop authority would protect her final earning years.
